comments.comment_body: Ciao Mattia, hai già provato a disegnare un linea interna dove dovrebbe crearsi la piegatura che si vede nella foto? Ciao Daniele. Grazie per la risposta. Non credo sia solo nelle linee di piegatura il problema. Non riesco a capire se il cartamodello della t-shirt oversize sia lo stesso della t-shirt base e sia sufficiente scalarlo o è un cartamodello un pò diverso? Riscontro enormi problemi nel giromanica se mi limito a scalare la dimensione del cartamodello base, non cade mai così dritta a piombo la spalla. Cosa ne pensi?

Mattia if you take the basic tee shirt pattern from the library and arrange it on the avatar &gt then simulate it on the avatar in the 'A' pose &gt at that point look at the shoulder length at that simulation and don't worry about the drape, what you want is the measure across the shoulder. Then measure once more on the avatar to where you want the tee shirt cap (sleeve) length to go to on the enlarged shirt (for example 10cm down the shoulder either side. Then use a simple calculation (divide the smaller cap length of the small teeshirt by the larger avatar measure ) and get a % increase. Then select all pattern pieces of the tee shirt and assign them a warp /weft percentage increase in the property editor to match the % increase (eg: 20%) you calculated earlier &gt warp/weft now at 120% = 20% increase in pattern size. This allows the 2D drafting of the patterns to remain fixed in the 2D drafting window (smaller size) but the actual simulation in the 3D window will now be greatly scaled up (eg: 120%) larger. Test this by draping the new tee-shirt (shrinkage increased) on the avatar for the arms in the 'A' position &gt see pose for arms slightly out. Then simulate the shirt at the larger shrinkage scale and use a pose motion to place the arms to the side from the 'A' pose position. That should give you a relatively quick way to scale any pattern experimentally using the shrinkage factor of warp/weft in the pattern piece property editor to test the overall size on the avatar - then just numerically adjust that until you have a tee shirt at the right scale under simulated drape and pose. When you are happy with that look at that value and decide if you want to make it permanent in the 2D pattern sizes &gt where you scale the 2D drafting to that same warp/weft ration using the 2D drafting scale tool and then zero the pattern shrinkage back to 100% for all patterns. This is how you perform a basic scaling of a garment to get some size variation quickly without effecting the drafting until you are sure you want to lock it in. Many simple patterns are scaled relative to multiple body datum lines - so for some simple clothing item like 'Tee shirts' which really only has the chest girth as a measured datum you can often get away with this for a quick size change, by simply using warp/weft shrinkage factors in the property editor.

Check out the CLO3D SDK

The software SDK integration has been around for some time (for mac and PC) over 18 months on the V5.0 version. If you do CNC embroidery at a production level relative to pattern pieces then you must appreciate that it is the production embroidery CNC data and datafile exchange with their respective vendors that drive the quality control of what can be made - and consequently it's simulation should mirror that. It is not the visual simulation in isolation. You should explore simply taking in the embroidery or bead work texture as a transparent .png with accompanying texture maps. And then you need to check that your embroidery CNC software can produce the visual simulation image maps at the same scale you need for use inside CLO3D. Then set your drafting symbol and insertion point notations to work on your 2D patterns. You can attach the CNC embroidery datafile as a file attachment with any project within the workspace. Embroidery CAD data-files are specific to pattern pieces. If you have good production embroidery you can generally output a high quality 3D texture simulation for that CNC data as image maps. There is no reason why you cannot apply that to any pattern piece at the textural level. It is therefore unnecessary to have a CNC dxf embroidery CAD tool within CLO3D, at that level of integration. If the visual simulation of the embroidery in CLO3D is the driver and not the CNC CAD data, then the image texture outputs at scale 1:1 and position on the pattern piece from production embroidery software is suffice. When you are drafting in CLO3D you can create a custom insertion point (baseline) on any pattern piece to denote the CNC cad position that relates to an attached dxf cnc embroidery datafle. The same goes for beading software, the CNC datafile and the visual outputs can be mutually exclusive and bound together in the techpack within the file attachment area of project work-spaces. All you need is a part code and item reference on the pattern and then lay the texture of the embroidery by it's insertion point. In that manner you can render the sample and still have the CNC datafile component under version control with the tech pack. If you look into the CLOSET workspace you will see there is a handy technical notes space for this, which is customary for detailing and specifying all trim and notions.

Oh! I figured it out. Using the Transform Pattern Tool, select the piece. This establishes the bounding box with a center point. If you hover over the center point it will instruct to "double click to activate pivot". When activated all bounding box points will turn orange. Then DRAG that center point to anywhere on the pattern piece or pattern perimeter and let go, then select the handle of the bounding box and the piece will rotate from the point you dragged. Warning, if you click off the pattern piece, you'll have to start over with double clicking the center point to reactive the "drag to pivot" option. Prior post: This isn't a true statement.
